claims.claim: Welleck and colleagues report that nucleus sampling too produced non-terminating sequences, at 0.06 per cent with the tanh-RNN and 0.13 per cent with the LSTM-RNN at a nucleus of 0.2.
claims.source: Welleck, Kulikov, Kim, Pang, Cho, arXiv:2002.02492v2 (2020)
claims.modelEra: tanh-RNN and LSTM-RNN, 2020; register measured: Wikitext-103 Wikipedia prose

claims.claim: Fu and colleagues argue that the repetition problem originates in properties of human language itself rather than in the model architecture or the sampling method.
claims.source: Fu, Lam, So, Shi, 'A Theoretical Analysis of the Repetition Problem in Text Generation', arXiv:2012.14660v4 (2021); AAAI 2021
claims.quote: caused by the traits of our language
claims.modelEra: Markov analysis with NMT and language-modelling experiments, 2020-2021; register measured: translation corpora and language modelling

claims.claim: Fu and colleagues name the high inflow problem, in which many different words predict the same next word with high probability, as the major cause of loops.
claims.source: Fu, Lam, So, Shi, arXiv:2012.14660v4 (2021); AAAI 2021
claims.quote: exist too many words predicting the same word as the
claims.modelEra: Markov generation model analysis, 2020-2021; register: NMT and language modelling

claims.claim: Meister, Vieira and Cotterell argue that beam search works because it enforces uniform information density, an even spread of surprisal across a sentence.
claims.source: Meister, Vieira, Cotterell, 'If Beam Search is the Answer, What was the Question?', arXiv:2010.02650v2 (2021); EMNLP 2020
claims.modelEra: neural machine translation models, IWSLT'14 and WMT'14, observation 2020; register measured: translated news and talks, not open-ended fiction

claims.claim: Meister, Vieira and Cotterell report that in their machine-translation experiments a lower standard deviation of per-sentence surprisal went with a higher BLEU score, an inverse relationship they take as evidence for the uniform information density property in good text.
claims.quote: is adhered to strongly correlates with BLEU
claims.modelEra: NMT transformer models on IWSLT'14 and WMT'14 Newstest2014, 2020; register measured: translated news, a constrained task rather than open-ended generation

claims.claim: Pillutla and colleagues report that MAUVE scores greedy decoding at .016 on web text from GPT-2 XL, the lowest of the three decoding algorithms they compare.
claims.source: Pillutla, Swayamdipta, Zellers, Thickstun, Welleck, Choi, Harchaoui, 'MAUVE', arXiv:2102.01454v3 (2021); NeurIPS 2021
claims.quote: the lowest quality to greedy decoding (.016)
claims.page: Section 4.1, 'MAUVE identifies quality differences between decoding algorithms'; Table 3
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 XL and Grover, observation 2021; register measured: web text, news and story continuations

claims.claim: Pillutla and colleagues report that nucleus sampling has a lower Type I error than ancestral sampling but a higher Type II error, meaning it fails to cover the spread of human text.
claims.source: Pillutla, Swayamdipta, Zellers, Thickstun, Welleck, Choi, Harchaoui, arXiv:2102.01454v3 (2021); NeurIPS 2021
claims.quote: nucleus sampling does not effectively cover the human text distribution
claims.modelEra: Grover and GPT-2, 2021; register measured: web text and news

claims.claim: Pillutla and colleagues state that some plausible human text simply cannot be produced by a truncation-based decoder such as nucleus sampling, which is the Type II error their measure is built to catch.
claims.source: Pillutla, Swayamdipta, Zellers, Thickstun, Welleck, Choi, Harchaoui, arXiv:2102.01454v3 (2021); NeurIPS 2021
claims.quote: cannot be generated by truncation-based decoding algorithms such as nucleus sampling

claims.claim: Pillutla and colleagues report a Spearman rank correlation of 0.952 between MAUVE and human human-likeness judgments on web text, against 0.810 for generation perplexity and minus 0.167 for the repetition metric.
claims.source: Pillutla, Swayamdipta, Zellers, Thickstun, Welleck, Choi, Harchaoui, arXiv:2102.01454v3 (2021); NeurIPS 2021
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 sizes with ancestral and nucleus sampling, 214 Mechanical Turk workers, 2021; register measured: web text

claims.claim: Zhang, Duckworth, Ippolito and Neelakantan report a likelihood trap: past an inflection point the sentences a model rates as most likely are rated by human crowdworkers as lower in quality.
claims.source: Zhang, Duckworth, Ippolito, Neelakantan, 'Trading Off Diversity and Quality in Natural Language Generation', arXiv:2004.10450v1 (2020)
claims.quote: the highest likelihood sentences are of surprisingly low
claims.modelEra: dialogue and open-ended generation models, 2020; register measured: conversational responses rated by crowdworkers

claims.claim: Zhang and colleagues based the likelihood trap finding on 146 crowdworkers rating 100 sentences drawn across a range of model likelihoods.
Zhang and colleagues report that once decoding algorithms are compared at equal entropy, the quality of their samples is comparable over a wide range, and they diverge only in the low-entropy regime.
claims.quote: when aligned on entropy, sample quality between all
claims.modelEra: 2020, twenty decoder-hyperparameter configurations; register measured: dialogue responses rated by crowdworkers

claims.claim: Zhang and colleagues report that in the low-entropy regime nucleus sampling beat top-k, which beat temperature sampling, on human quality ratings.
Zhang and colleagues' decoder comparison rests on over 38,000 paired ratings of almost 10,000 samples.
Nadeem, He, Cho and Glass report that top-k, nucleus and tempered sampling perform on a par with one another in their human quality-diversity evaluation.
claims.source: Nadeem, He, Cho, Glass, 'A Systematic Characterization of Sampling Algorithms for Open-ended Language Generation', arXiv:2009.07243v1 (2020); AACL-IJCNLP 2020
claims.quote: are on par with each other
claims.modelEra: GPT2-small 110M fine-tuned on Gigaword and Wikitext-103, 602 Mechanical Turk crowdworkers, 2020; register measured: news sentences and Wikipedia prose

verdicts.trueWording: "Nucleus sampling also produced non-terminating sequences with the tanh-RNN" (§5.1)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2002.02492v2 -> pdftotext -layout. Quote exact. Sentence continues with (0.06%, nuc-0.2) for tanh-RNN and (0.13%, nuc-0.2) for LSTM-RNN; Table 1 row nucleus-0.2 gives 0.06+/-0.02 and 0.13+/-0.15, mean over 10 initializations. Every limb supported. Register caveat: this experiment is Wikitext2, not Wikitext-103 as the claim's modelEra field states (Wikitext-103 is used only for the separate GPT-2 transformer experiment) - the claim sentence itself does not name a corpus, so the verdict stands.

verdicts.trueWording: "caused by the traits of our language itself" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2012.14660v4. Quote exact in Abstract. Conclusion repeats it in other words: theory shows the problem is caused by the language itself. The 'rather than architecture or sampling method' limb is the paper's own framing: the Introduction lists those two as prior conjectures whose real cause was 'still unknown', and the Abstract casts existing sampling methods as minimizing the upper bounds (remedies), not causes.

verdicts.trueWording: "exist too many words predicting the same word as the subsequent" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2012.14660v4. Quote exact. Abstract: 'One major reason is attributed to' that fact, and 'it is easy to go back to that word and form repetitions and we dub it as the high inflow problem'. Both the naming limb and the major-cause limb are supported verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "beam search enforces uniform information density in text" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2010.02650v2. Quote exact in the Abstract, where the finding is credited to a property motivated by cognitive science. Section 4.1 is titled 'The UID Bias in Beam Search'. The 'even spread of surprisal' gloss matches Hypothesis 4.1, which has speakers distributing information uniformly across the signal, with surprisal as the paper's information measure throughout Section 6.

verdicts.trueWording: "a strong inverse relationship between BLEU and average standard deviation" (§6.1)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2010.02650v2. Abstract quote exact. §6.1 Exact Decoding: 'Fig. 1 also shows a strong inverse relationship between BLEU and average standard deviation (per sentence) of surprisals. We take these observations as empirical validation of Hyp. 4.2.' Direction (lower sigma with higher BLEU), the per-sentence unit, and the evidential use all confirmed. Datasets IWSLT'14 De-En and WMT'14 En-Fr with Newstest'14 test set, matching modelEra.

Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01454v3. Quote exact. Table 3 caption reads 'web text, GPT-2 xl'; appendix Table 6 xl block confirms greedy MAUVE 0.016 (vs sampling 0.882, nucleus 0.940). Adversarial check on 'lowest of the three': the paper's sentence compares exactly greedy/ancestral/nucleus, and greedy .016 is also below the fourth (adversarial, .057), so the limb is true either way.

verdicts.trueWording: "nucleus sampling does not effectively cover the human text distribution" (Fig. 2)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01454v3. Quote exact in the Figure 2 caption. That caption calls the Type I error 'slightly smaller' than ancestral sampling's and the Type II error higher, so the claim's 'lower' is accurate and drops only the hedge. The caption scopes the comparison to Grover base (rightmost panel); the claim names no model, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: "cannot be generated by truncation-based decoding algorithms such as nucleus sampling" (§2)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01454v3. Quote exact. The sentence opens by defining Type II errors as false negatives and gives this inability as the example, so the Type II attribution is explicit rather than inferred; it is formalized immediately below under 'Quantifying the Errors', where KL(P|Q) quantifies the Type II error. The quote sits a few lines above that heading rather than inside it, which does not affect support.

verdicts.trueWording: Table 5 Human-like/BT web text: MAUVE .952, Gen. PPL .810, REP -.167
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01454v3. Claim supplied no quote, so verbatim grading does not apply; all three figures match Table 5 row 'Human-like/BT, Web text' exactly, and the body text repeats 'how human-like (0.952)'. §4.3 confirms the measure is a Spearman rank correlation against fitted Bradley-Terry coefficients from 214 Mechanical Turk workers, matching modelEra. Note for downstream use: MAUVE's 'Interesting/BT' correlation is also 0.810, a coincidence that could be misread; the claim's 0.810 is correctly the Gen. PPL cell of the human-like row.

verdicts.trueWording: "the highest likelihood sentences are of surprisingly low quality" (§1)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2004.10450v1. Quote exact in §1. The inflection-point limb comes from the Figure 1 caption: log likelihoods are generally positively correlated with average human quality judgments, with 'an inflection point after which they become negatively correlated'. Raters are crowdworkers (146 AMT workers).

verdicts.trueWording: "We asked 146 crowdworkers to rate the quality of 100 sentences" (Fig. 1)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2004.10450v1. Quote exact; the caption continues 'across a variety of model likelihoods', supporting the range limb, and each plotted point averages 5 sentences of similar likelihood. §4.1 confirms the same qualified pool of 146 AMT workers.

verdicts.trueWording: "when aligned on entropy, sample quality between all autoregressive decoding algorithms" (§4.2)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2004.10450v1. Quote exact; the sentence completes with the samples being comparable across a wide range. The divergence limb is the next sentence, which states that algorithms' sample quality diverges only when entropy is low. Twenty decoding algorithm-hyperparameter configurations confirmed in Section 4.2, matching modelEra.

verdicts.trueWording: "nucleus sampling outperforms top-k, which in turn outperforms temperature sampling" (§4.2)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2004.10450v1. Claim supplied no quote, so verbatim grading does not apply; the page states the ordering in almost these words, scoped to 'this regime' - the low-entropy regime named in the preceding sentence. Quality is the human pairwise preference score of §4.1 (workers rate five samples per prompt), supporting the 'human quality ratings' limb.

Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2004.10450v1. Quote exact in §1. §4.2 restates it with the 'paired' qualifier the claim uses: 'workers rate nearly 10,000 samples resulting in over 38,000 paired ratings.' Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "are on par with each other" (Figure 1 caption)
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arxiv.org/pdf/2009.07243v1. Quote exact. Figure 1 is explicitly the human evaluation panel ('Human evaluation (y-axis: quality, x-axis: diversity)'), so the 'human quality-diversity evaluation' limb holds; §1 names the three algorithms (top-k, nucleus, tempered) as performing on par in the Q-D trade-off 'as shown in Figure 1', and the Conclusion repeats it. §5.1 compares them by both automatic and human evaluation. 602 crowdworkers and the Gigaword/Wikitext-103 GPT2-small setup confirmed.
